newsitem.title: TAIWAN: BASEBALL-TAIWAN POLICE ACCUSED OF PLAYER BLACKMAIL.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-TAIWAN POLICE ACCUSED OF PLAYER BLACKMAIL.

text.p: Taiwan prosecutors on Wednesday detained two police officers suspected of blackmailing several baseball players to throw games for money in the latest gambling scandal to rock the professional league.

The two officers allegedly brought handguns to team dugouts during several 1996 games and coerced players to fix games so they could win money to pay off gambling debts, a Taipei investigation bureau prosecutor said by telephone.
"They (the officers) were friends with a person who ran an illegal gambling joint that apparently many of the players went to," said the prosecutor, who declined to be identified.
"Our sources told us the officers brought guns to force the players to throw games for paying off gambling debts," he said.
The alleged gambling centre operator, identified as Lee Mo-fa, was arrested in February, the prosecutor said.
He declined to identify the detained officers.

The reputation of Taiwan's eight-year-old baseball league suffered a major blow recently when prosecutors alleged that many players and coaches -- including its 1996 most valuable player -- threw games to earn kickbacks from gangsters.
Eight players, including 1996 MVP pitcher Kuo Chin-hsing, have been detained for alleged involvement in gambling.
Prosecutors have said they were investigating 22 others.

A newspaper poll published on February 23 showed that most Taiwan baseball fans felt they were being "cheated" when they watched the island's professional games, and did not believe authorities could ever eliminate game-fixing.
The league admits that some 1996 games were manipulated and has asked the Justice Ministry to investigate 13 games in which league officials suspected "irregular" on-field activities.
Daniel Tu, head of the main Chinese Professional Baseball League, has urged authorities to legalise sports betting to thwart game-fixing by organised crime syndicates.
Taiwan bans all gambling, but several senior officials -- including Vice-President Lien Chan -- have urged legalisation so authorities can better monitor betting and spot cheating.

Aside from the game-fixing within its own ranks, the Chinese Professional Baseball League faces a new challenge from the fledgling Taiwan Major League, which has poached many of the older leagues star players.
Both leagues began their 1997 seasons on February 28.
